title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences
claim: The classical divergence blows up as noise vanishes, while our transport-based variants stay finite and well-behaved.
layout: 1 log-scale line plot, three colored curves, legend top, marked limit point
description: A single line plot with a logarithmic y-axis from 10^-1 to 10^2. The x-axis is the noise variance sigma squared, from 0 to about 5.5. A legend box across the top lists three divergences between two Gaussians with equal covariance: KL in blue, D^KW with lambda=1 in red, and WKL in orange. The blue KL curve shoots up toward about 50 as sigma squared approaches 0, then decays slowly. The orange WKL curve is a flat horizontal line. The red D^KW curve starts at the same value as WKL and decreases smoothly, ending below KL. A black dot at sigma squared = 0 marks the finite limit, labeled 1/2 ||Delta m||_2^2 on the y-axis. The eye goes first to the steep blue divergence at the left edge.

abstract: Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization is widely used in reinforcement learning, but it becomes infinite under support mismatch and can degenerate in low-noise regimes. Using a unified information-geometric framework, we introduce KL analogs by replacing the Fisher-Rao geometry in the dynamical formulation of the KL with transport-based geometries, and derive closed-form expressions for common distribution families. Between elliptic distributions, these divergences remain finite for degenerating equal covariances and yield a geometric interpretation of regularization heuristics used in Kalman ensemble methods. We demonstrate the utility of these divergences in KL-regularized optimal control. In the fully tractable setting of linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise, the classical KL reduces to a quadratic control penalty that becomes singular as process noise vanishes. Our variants remove this singularity and yield well-posed problems. In both the double integrator and cart-pole examples, the resulting controls preserve nontrivial feedback and achieve better closed-loop performance.
